issues.detail: Projected difficulty proportions from the real set (35:20:8 for levels 1:2:3) to a 7-item test give expected counts of approximately 4–5 level-1, 2–3 level-2, and 1 level-3 items. The generated set has {"1":4,"2":2,"3":1}, which is within one item per level and thus numerically acceptable, but several items are mis-leveled relative to their actual cognitive demand, so the effective difficulty distribution is skewed too easy overall.

Items labeled as difficulty 2 or 3 often require only single-step recall or plug-and-chug reasoning typical of level 1–2. In particular, optics-b-generated-005 (conceptual description of a single polarizer) is closer to level 1–low 2; optics-b-generated-006 (thin lens with object at 2f) is a standard textbook example and should be level 1; optics-b-generated-007 (double-slit fringe spacing with proportional reasoning) is at most level 2, not 3.

The generated set omits several major topic clusters present in the calibration examples and expected for a Division B Optics written test: human eye and vision (including myopia/hyperopia and corrective lenses), color and spectra, photon/quantum line spectra (e.g., Balmer/Rydberg), quantitative Snell’s law and critical angle/TIR calculations, and quantitative mirror/lens image-distance and magnification problems. Coverage is therefore not proportional to the source set.

Three of seven items (003, 005, 007) are on physical optics (diffraction/interference/polarization), which is a heavier fraction than in the calibration set and crowds out geometric optics and eye/vision content.

Several items are generic, first-exposure textbook questions rather than competition-calibrated problems. For example, 001 (identify refraction at an interface), 002 (real/inverted image on a screen), and 004 (image distance in a plane mirror) are extremely standard and do not incorporate multi-step reasoning, parameter variation, or subtle misconceptions that would better match Science Olympiad style.

Multiple stems are wordier than necessary for their cognitive level, especially 001, 003, 004, 006, and 007. They include narrative detail and repeated clarifications (e.g., sign-convention notes, restating that the setup is in air, or that the pattern is visible) that do not materially affect the physics. This is more verbose than typical for Division B written tests at these difficulty levels.

Some multiple-choice items have distractors that are too obviously wrong for the intended level. For example, in 001, scattering is not a plausible alternative given the described sharp beam; in 002, a real image on a screen is almost always inverted, making the other options weak; in 004, 0.0 m and 0.4 m behind the mirror are easily eliminated by any student familiar with plane mirrors. This reduces discrimination and effective difficulty.

The set lacks the breadth of quantitative and applied problems seen in the calibration examples (e.g., diopter/eye-power calculations, Snell’s law numerics, Brewster’s angle, Rydberg formula). Most items are single-concept recognition or simple proportional reasoning. As a result, the test does not faithfully reflect the style and rigor of a 2025 Division B Optics written test, even allowing for a short 7-item representative subset.

optics-b-generated-001: Very basic identification of refraction with an overlong stem and weak distractors; better suited as an introductory worksheet item than a competition question.
optics-b-generated-003: Conceptually fine but framed as a generic diffraction grating question; no quantitative or multi-step reasoning, and the long description adds little beyond “white light through many closely spaced lines.”
optics-b-generated-004: Trivial plane-mirror distance question with unnecessary narrative detail and little challenge; difficulty is closer to 0–0.5.
optics-b-generated-005: Good concept (Malus’s law / polarization) but only asks for a qualitative explanation; no numerical intensity fraction or angle dependence, so it underuses the topic’s potential for level-2/3 rigor.
optics-b-generated-006: Classic 2f object distance for a converging lens; the answer (image at 2f, inverted) is standard and nearly rote for anyone who has seen lens diagrams. Marked as difficulty 2 but functions as difficulty 1.
optics-b-generated-007: Uses the standard y ∝ 1/d relation for double-slit spacing; once students recall the proportionality, the arithmetic is trivial (6 mm × 0.20/0.30 = 4 mm). For Division B, this is more like a solid level-2 item than level 3 and does not match the multi-step or conceptual subtlety of the calibration level-3 questions.
